Fresh research this session. authorities.name: W T Ramsay Ltd v Inland Revenue Commissioners
authorities.date_note: Judgment 1981, reported 1982 - a citation-year gap explained by publication lag, not an error.
authorities.proposition: Fiscal legislation must be construed purposively rather than through a purely linguistic, step-by-step analysis of a transaction's individual legal components. Where a scheme comprises a pre-planned, self-cancelling series of steps forming a single composite transaction, the tax statute applies to the commercial/economic effect of the transaction as a whole, not to each artificial step in isolation - a loss or gain arising at one stage of an indivisible, pre-ordained process and cancelled out at a later stage is not the kind of loss or gain the legislation targets.
authorities.verification_note: Predates the neutral-citation system and Find Case Law's coverage entirely - no direct primary-source fetch was attempted for that reason. Verified via UBS AG v HMRC [2016] UKSC 13 (below), which quotes Lord Wilberforce's holding directly with a page pincite (p 326) at paragraph 62, plus an independent full-text transcript (uniset.ca) and a Practical Law case entry corroborating the case name, citation, and panel.

authorities.name: UBS AG v Commissioners for HMRC; DB Group Services (UK) Ltd v Commissioners for HMRC
authorities.judge_or_panel: Lord Reed (sole judgment; Lord Neuberger, Lord Mance, Lord Carnwath, Lord Hodge agreeing)
authorities.proposition: Restates the Ramsay approach as the ordinary modern purposive method of statutory construction applied to tax statutes: give the provision a purposive construction to identify the nature of transaction it targets, then ask whether the actual transaction - viewed realistically, considering the overall effect of elements intended to operate together - answers that statutory description. Elements inserted into a composite transaction with no business or commercial purpose other than attracting a tax exemption will often be disregarded for fiscal purposes, depending on the true construction of the specific provision. Applied to elaborate bank bonus-avoidance share schemes (UBS's FTSE-100-trigger scheme, Deutsche Bank's leaver-condition scheme), which failed to qualify for the intended income-tax exemption because the restrictive conditions attached to the shares had no genuine commercial rationale - they existed solely to trigger the exemption.
authorities.verification_note: Fetched live and directly from Find Case Law this session, independently re-fetched and re-confirmed a second time - both fetches consistent on paragraph 62's Ramsay-extension holding. A direct PDF fetch from supremecourt.uk failed to decode in this environment's tools; Find Case Law was used successfully instead.

edges.verified_via: UBS AG v HMRC [2016] UKSC 13, paras 62-63 and 98, fetched directly from Find Case Law and independently re-confirmed: restates and applies the Ramsay purposive-construction approach, criticising the Court of Appeal below for adopting a literal construction instead.

what_this_is_not: Two verified nodes covering the Ramsay principle and its modern restatement. Does not cover the General Anti-Abuse Rule (Finance Act 2013 Part 5 - a candidate statute checked this session but abandoned after an unverifiable amendment claim surfaced, not included here), income tax/corporation tax/VAT substantive rules, or any other Tax Law subject - all remain unbuilt.
